chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## A Company Remade

In the fourth quarter of 2025, Nebius Group's core AI cloud segment grew 802% year-on-year. Total group revenue for the quarter reached $227.7 million — itself a 547% increase over the prior-year period — and the company exited the year with an annualised revenue run-rate of $1.25 billion and $3.7 billion in cash on its balance sheet. These are not the numbers of a company finding its footing; they are the numbers of a company attempting to compress a decade of infrastructure build into roughly eighteen months.

Nebius Group N.V. trades on the NASDAQ under the ticker NBIS. It is incorporated in the Netherlands and files with the SEC on a 20-F foreign-private-issuer basis, supplemented by 6-K quarterly disclosures. Its chief executive is Arkady Volozh, who founded the company that became Yandex in 2000, led it through its 2011 NASDAQ listing and its years as Russia's dominant internet group, stepped down in 2022 under political pressure following the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and returned to the role in 2024 as part of the corporate restructuring that gave the surviving listed entity its current form.

Nebius Group is the Netherlands-domiciled successor to Yandex N.V., reconstituted through a 2024 restructuring that separated the Russian operating business and refocused the surviving parent on AI infrastructure. Alongside the core AI cloud business, the group retains three smaller branded subsidiaries: Toloka AI, which provides human-data labelling for AI training pipelines; TripleTen, an online technology education platform; and Avride, which is developing autonomous driving technology.

## The FY2025 Print

The headline Q4 metrics capture only part of the structural picture. Nebius reported a Q4 net loss of $249.6 million — reflecting the depreciation and stock-compensation weight of a scale-up at speed — but the more consequential line was operating cash flow: $834 million in a single quarter against revenue of $227.7 million. The gap is the customer-prepayment signature. Enterprise AI compute customers, structured like hyperscaler counterparties, prepay for capacity, generating cash ahead of recognised revenue. Nebius was, in the fourth quarter, collecting at nearly four times the rate it was recognising.

Capital expenditure of approximately $2 billion in Q4 alone — a roughly 9x capex-to-revenue ratio — illustrates the build-ahead posture. At year-end, Nebius had 170 megawatts of power actively connected to its data centre footprint, against more than 2 gigawatts under contract. The gap between active and contracted capacity is the physical expression of the investment thesis: the company has secured the grid connections and real estate it believes demand will fill, and is now in the process of filling them.

| Metric | Q4 2025 |
|---|---|
| Revenue | $227.7M |
| YoY growth (total) | +547% |
| YoY growth (core AI cloud) | +802% |
| Net loss | $249.6M |
| Operating cash flow | $834M |
| Capex (approx.) | ~$2.0B |
| Exit ARR | $1.25B |
| Exit cash | $3.7B |
| Active power | 170 MW |
| Contracted power | >2,000 MW |

## The FY2026 Commitment

Management's guidance for 2026 is, by any peer comparison, the most aggressive public commitment in the AI-cloud sector. [Nebius Q4 2025 earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) puts full-year revenue at $3.0–3.4 billion — implying roughly seven times FY2025 — with an adjusted EBITDA margin target of approximately 40% at the core segment level, capital expenditure of $16–20 billion, and exit ARR of $7–9 billion with more than half of that figure already contracted at the time of guidance. Connected power is targeted at 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt by year-end, a five-to-six-fold physical expansion in a single calendar year.

The contracted-ARR disclosure is the detail that distinguishes guidance from aspiration: Nebius is not projecting $7–9 billion on the basis of pipeline or addressable market; it is stating that the majority of that figure rests on executed customer commitments.

## The Strategic Equity Signal

In August 2025, Nebius closed a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement with three named participants: Accel, Nvidia, and Orbis Investments. The Nvidia component is particularly loaded — Nvidia is simultaneously Nebius's primary GPU supplier and a balance-sheet investor, an alignment of commercial and financial interest that would be difficult to replicate with a competing hardware vendor. Accel's Matt Weigand, a partner since 2013 with a background in enterprise software and security, held observer rights ahead of the August 2025 AGM and was subsequently elected to the board.

## The Central Tension

The question that Nebius's FY2026 commitment poses — and that no equity filing can answer — is whether Volozh's team can convert more than fifty percent of contracted ARR into deployed capacity inside the guidance window. The constraint is not financial: $3.7 billion in cash plus $834 million of Q4 operating cash flow plus the $700 million strategic placement provides the funding base. The constraint is operational: five-to-six-fold power expansion, GPU procurement at scale through a supplier who is also a shareholder, concurrent real estate and utility execution across multiple jurisdictions, and customer ramp management — all while CoreWeave, Lambda Labs, Crusoe, and the hyperscalers' own internal AI cloud capacity absorb the same enterprise compute demand Nebius is contracting. The Nvidia strategic alignment offers a procurement advantage that few peers can replicate. Whether that advantage translates into executed megawatts by December 2026 is the question the operating record will settle.

chapters.title: From CompTek to Yandex to Nebius
chapters.body:
## The CompTek seed

The entity that would eventually become Nebius Group N.V. had its earliest origins not in a search algorithm but in a computer-hardware distribution business. In 1990, John Boynton co-founded CompTek International in Moscow — one of the first generation of commercially oriented technology companies to emerge from the collapsing Soviet system. CompTek's role in the subsequent decade was less that of a technology developer than a corporate nursery: it provided the infrastructure, early capital, and operational scaffolding within which Arkady Volozh and his collaborators built and incubated what would become Russia's dominant internet search engine.

Yandex as a named search product launched in 1997, and the company was formally incorporated in 2000. The ownership and board connections forged in the CompTek incubator persisted directly into the incorporated Yandex entity. Boynton joined the Yandex board at inception in 2000 and did not leave it — serving through every phase of the company's subsequent history and assuming the chairmanship in 2016. His tenure represents the longest unbroken thread of institutional memory in what is now the Nebius Group governance structure.

The second foundational financial connection was forged in 1998, when Charles Ryan — then co-founder and chief executive of United Financial Group, one of the leading Russia-focused investment banks of the post-Soviet era — sponsored an early-stage technology investment through ru-Net Holdings that included Yandex. Ryan had previously led the St. Petersburg privatisation programme for the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development; UFG would later be acquired in its entirety by Deutsche Bank, with Ryan serving as Deutsche Bank Group's chief country officer and CEO for Russia from 2005 to 2008. He joined the Yandex board at the 2011 NASDAQ IPO and remained a director through the full arc of the company's subsequent transformation.

## The dominant decade and the 2022 break

Yandex's 2011 NASDAQ IPO raised approximately $1.3 billion and valued the company at roughly $8 billion, at the time one of the largest internet IPOs since Google. The listing reflected a business that by 2011 controlled more than sixty per cent of Russian internet search — a market-share position it held, and in some periods extended, through the following decade. The 2010s saw Yandex diversify aggressively beyond search: ride-hailing through Yandex.Taxi (a joint venture with Uber that eventually became Yandex.Go), food delivery through Yandex.Eats, cloud infrastructure, self-driving technology through Yandex Self-Driving Group, and the broader ecosystem of verticals that characterised the dominant internet platform model of the era. By the early 2020s Yandex was the most complete Russian-language internet ecosystem in existence, with a NASDAQ-listed equity that gave Western institutional capital indirect exposure to Russian consumer internet growth.

Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine ended that proposition. The political and sanctions pressures that followed created an impossible position for a company incorporated in the Netherlands, listed in New York, and operationally headquartered in Moscow. Volozh stepped down as chief executive in June 2022 — a resignation that he later described, in the context of his public distancing from the invasion, as part of a broader personal and corporate reckoning. He remained connected to the ownership and board structure, but the operational leadership of the company changed hands at a moment of acute external pressure.

## Restructuring and rebirth: 2024

The solution that emerged over the following two years was a structural separation of the listed parent from the Russian operating business. In 2024, Yandex N.V. completed what was, in corporate-transaction terms, a substantial divestiture: the entire Russian operating business — the search engine, Yandex.Taxi, the food delivery platforms, the Russian cloud, and the adjacent domestic products — was sold to a consortium of Russian investors. The Netherlands-domiciled parent retained the international assets and was rebranded Nebius Group N.V., continuing to trade on NASDAQ under the new ticker NBIS. Volozh returned as chief executive to lead the refocused group.

The board was reconfigured to match the new strategic identity. Boynton remained as chairman and Ryan as an independent director — the two longest-serving outside directors, whose combined institutional knowledge gave the post-restructuring entity continuity and credibility with long-term shareholders.

## The post-restructuring board build

Ophir Nave joined as chief operating officer in May 2024 and was elected as an executive director at the August 2024 general meeting. His profile was calibrated precisely for the legal-architecture complexity of the restructuring: a Doctor of Juridical Science from Harvard Law School, a clerkship at the Israeli Supreme Court, a period at Wachtell Lipton Rosen & Katz in New York, and a lead partnership in the corporate and M&A practice at Arnon Tadmor-Levy in Israel. The assembly of a Netherlands-incorporated public company retaining international technology assets from a Russian operating entity while maintaining a NASDAQ listing is a feat of cross-border legal engineering; Nave's credential set is the explanation for how it was executed.

Elena Bunina joined as a non-executive director at the same August 2024 meeting. A mathematician with nearly seventy published research papers, she had previously served as general director of human resources and head of academic and educational services across the Yandex Group until April 2022. At Nebius she leads science and education, connecting directly to the TripleTen subsidiary.

Kira Radinsky joined as an independent non-executive director in 2024, bringing the board's most directly AI-domain-aligned credential: chief executive of Diagnostic Robotics and founder of Mana Bio. Radinsky previously co-founded SalesPredict, acquired by eBay in 2016. Her addition signalled the governance transformation from a Russia-focused internet conglomerate to an AI-infrastructure company.

At the August 2025 annual general meeting, two further directors were elected. Arne Grimme, a partner at De Brauw Blackstone Westbroek and head of its corporate M&A practice, provided the Netherlands-domicile legal anchor. Matthew Weigand, a partner at Accel, joined concurrent with the close of Nebius's $700 million strategic equity placement. The resulting eight-director board reads as a precise mapping of the strategic transformation: founder continuity plus legal architecture plus AI domain expertise plus Dutch corporate governance plus venture-co-investor oversight.

## The inflection and what it means

The thirty-six-year arc from a Moscow hardware-distribution company to a NASDAQ-listed AI cloud operator is, at one level, an improbable straight line. At another, it is a precise illustration of what corporate restructuring can produce when the post-divestiture entity retains the institutional knowledge, the financial resources, and a founder willing to rebuild. The corporate history of Nebius Group is not prologue to the investment thesis — it is the investment thesis. The balance-sheet reconstitution, the board reconfiguration, and the Nvidia strategic relationship are all outputs of a restructuring executed with enough speed and legal precision to catch the AI infrastructure cycle before the window narrowed. Whether the FY2026 capacity ramp can be delivered inside the guidance window is the question that dominates every subsequent chapter of this analysis; the corporate-history answer is that the organisational capability to attempt it was assembled more rapidly, and from more adverse starting conditions, than any comparable transformation in the current AI-infrastructure cohort.

chapters.title: Core AI cloud plus three branded subsidiaries
chapters.body:
## The Four-Part Architecture

The Nebius portfolio comprises four distinct businesses, each operating under its own brand. The largest by revenue and strategic weight is the core AI cloud — GPU-powered compute infrastructure sold to AI labs, enterprise model developers, and multi-cloud buyers. Around it sit three wholly owned subsidiaries: Toloka AI (human-data labelling), TripleTen (online tech education), and Avride (autonomous driving research). Understanding how those four pieces fit together — and which one is doing the work — is the starting point for any serious analysis of the NBIS equity.

## Core AI Cloud: The Dominant Revenue Engine

The core AI cloud segment was, by Q4 2025, the only unit growing fast enough to shape the group's financial trajectory. [Nebius Group Q4 and FY2025 Results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) showed the gap between the +802% segment growth rate and the +547% consolidated rate — meaning the subsidiary businesses were diluting headline growth.

The business is deliberately full-stack. Nebius procures Nvidia GPU hardware (H100 and H200 generations) and deploys them inside data centers it designs and operates. The stack extends through cooling infrastructure, high-bandwidth networking interconnects, operating-system-level software, and developer-facing interfaces. Customer access comes through two pathways: Nebius AI Studio (self-service platform for smaller model-training teams) and direct enterprise contracting for multi-year committed workloads.

The geographic footprint at FY2025 close was predominantly European. Legacy data center infrastructure in Finland formed the earliest operational base. US expansion was underway through 2025, though specific site locations were not disclosed.

The contracted-power picture tells the capacity story: 170 megawatts of active power at year-end 2025, against more than 2,000 megawatts contracted — representing either an extraordinary forward-commitment book or, depending on execution confidence, the single largest operational risk on the balance sheet.

The Nvidia relationship is the structural variable that distinguishes Nebius from most peers. With Nvidia as both primary GPU supplier and equity investor (via the August 2025 placement), Nebius carries an implied allocation-priority advantage during periods of constrained supply — though specific GPU allocation volumes were not publicly disclosed.

## Toloka AI: The Data-Labelling Complement

Toloka AI operates a crowd-sourced human-data-labelling platform serving AI model developers who need ground-truth annotation for vision, language, and multimodal training datasets. Under Nebius ownership, Toloka is positioned as complementary: customers building AI models frequently need both compute and annotated training data. Toloka competes with Scale AI, Surge AI, and proprietary annotation operations run by the major AI labs. Separate revenue figures were not disclosed in available segment reporting.

## TripleTen: The Education Vertical

TripleTen is the most conventionally consumer-facing subsidiary, offering online bootcamp-style courses in data science, software engineering, and AI/ML skills. The strategic rationale for retention is less obvious than for Toloka: tech education has its own competitive dynamics (Coursera, Udemy, university extension programs), and the revenue profile is unlikely to scale proportionally to the AI cloud core. Management had not publicly indicated plans to separate TripleTen as of the snapshot date.

## Avride: The Long-Cycle Moonshot

Avride is the business furthest from near-term commercial relevance. The autonomous driving and robotics platform is characterised as a long-cycle R&D holding. It consumed capital in pursuit of technical milestones and contributed no material revenue to FY2025 consolidated results. The group's retention reflects the talent and IP base inherited from Yandex's self-driving research program. Avride's path to monetisation remains unresolved.

## Revenue Mix and Disclosure Constraints

The segment architecture is clear at the product-brand level. The revenue arithmetic is not. Nebius did not separately disclose revenue for Toloka, TripleTen, or Avride. The +802% Q4 YoY growth rate for the core AI cloud segment implied that segment substantially dominated the consolidated print.

| Metric | Q4 2025 | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Group revenue | $227.7M | $3.0–3.4B |
| Core AI cloud YoY growth | +802% | Not separately guided |
| Annualised run rate (ARR) | $1.25B exit-2025 | $7–9B |
| ARR contracted share | — | >50% |
| Active power | 170MW | 800–1,000MW |
| Capex | ~$2B (Q4 only) | $16–20B |

[Source: Nebius Group Q4 and FY2025 Results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results)

## Structural Position: The Advantages and the Asymmetric Risk

The balance-sheet endowment is genuinely unusual in its competitive set. $3.7 billion of cash at year-end 2025, augmented by $834 million Q4 operating cash flow, provides a funding runway that no pure-play AI cloud competitor without direct balance-sheet backing can replicate. CoreWeave accessed debt markets at scale; Nebius entered FY2026 with equity capital already in place.

The structural disadvantage is the starting position — ramping from a post-restructuring base rather than a multi-year operating history. The gap between active and contracted capacity requires simultaneous execution across power utility agreements, real estate, GPU delivery schedules, construction, and customer onboarding — in multiple geographies, in a single fiscal year. That execution complexity is the primary risk embedded in FY2026 guidance.

chapters.title: $3.7B cash and the $20B capex bar
chapters.body:
## The FY2025 Inflection

When Nebius published its fourth-quarter 2025 results on 12 February 2026, the numbers removed any remaining ambiguity about ambitions. [Q4 revenue came in at $227.7 million, up 547 percent year-on-year](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results). The core AI cloud segment grew 802 percent. The company exited the year with an annualised revenue run rate of $1.25 billion and $3.7 billion of cash on the balance sheet. In the final quarter alone, Nebius deployed approximately $2 billion of capital expenditure. Active connected power reached 170 megawatts against more than 2 gigawatts under contract.

The quarter's revenue figure came in below consensus expectations of roughly $247 million. That miss mattered less than the direction of travel. Guidance for FY2026 — revenue of $3 to $3.4 billion, capital expenditure of $16 to $20 billion, ARR of $7 to $9 billion with more than half already contracted — was the most aggressive full-year commitment any publicly listed AI cloud company had issued.

## The Prepayment Signature

The most structurally important disclosure in the Q4 print was not on the income statement. [Operating cash flow for the quarter totalled $834 million against reported revenue of $227.7 million](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm) — a ratio of approximately 3.7 times.

That gap is the fingerprint of hyperscaler-style customer prepayment. Enterprise customers paying for future GPU compute capacity in advance generate cash immediately; that cash is recorded as deferred revenue and recognised only when capacity is consumed. At Nebius, the Q4 ratio indicated a substantial book of forward commitments had been signed and partially funded heading into 2026.

When management described more than 50 percent of the $7 to $9 billion ARR target as already contracted, they were projecting from signed agreements with cash-deposit mechanics already in motion. The operating cash flow dynamics corroborated that characterisation.

## Walking the Guidance Arithmetic

| Metric | FY2025 Reference | FY2026 Guidance | Implied Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $227.7M (Q4 run-rate) | $3.0–$3.4B | ~7× FY25 |
| ARR (exit) | $1.25B | $7–$9B | 5.6–7.2× |
| Capex | ~$2B (Q4 alone) | $16–$20B | — |
| Connected power | 170 MW | 800 MW–1 GW | 4.7–5.9× |
| Adj. EBITDA margin | 24% (Q4 2025) | ~40% | +16 pp |
| Contracted ARR share | — | >50% | — |

[Source: Nebius Q4 2025 6-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm)

The revenue guidance implies approximately seven times FY2025 revenue at the midpoint. That growth rate requires contracted-ARR coverage already embedded in the signed book to convert into delivered capacity and recognised revenue on schedule.

The ARR target of $7 to $9 billion is a forward-looking exit figure — the run rate intended by 31 December 2026. If exit ARR reaches the $8 billion midpoint, Q4 2026 revenue would approach $2 billion in a single quarter.

## The Capex Arithmetic

Capital expenditure of $16 to $20 billion for FY2026 against projected revenue of $3 to $3.4 billion is a capex-to-revenue ratio of 4.7 to 6.7 times — a ratio with no parallel in publicly listed AI cloud infrastructure at this revenue baseline.

Nebius is constructing capacity ahead of demand — acquiring and fitting out data centre facilities, executing GPU procurement with Nvidia, and activating power utility agreements simultaneously. In Q4 2025 alone, approximately $2 billion was deployed against $227.7 million of revenue: a 9x single-quarter ratio. The FY2026 guidance implies this pace will accelerate. On a straight-line basis, $16 to $20 billion over four quarters averages $4 to $5 billion per quarter — double to two-and-a-half times the Q4 2025 rate.

The build-ahead-of-demand model is structurally sound only if contracted ARR converts. Infrastructure purchased to fulfil commitments that slip or cancel becomes stranded depreciation.

## The Financing Stack

At year-end 2025, Nebius held $3.7 billion in cash and liquid equivalents. That figure reflected the August 2025 $700 million strategic equity placement alongside conversion of contracted ARR into advance-payment receipts.

Against a capex guidance of $16 to $20 billion, the $3.7 billion position covers 18 to 23 percent of the range. Management acknowledged explicitly that the capex programme exceeded cash on hand and that additional financing — through prepayments, potential debt, or further equity — would be required.

The strategic-investor structure of the August 2025 placement reframed the equity story at a critical moment. An oversubscribed close with Accel, Nvidia, and Orbis provided a de facto validation certificate from the infrastructure investment community when market credibility was most consequential.

## The Margin Mechanics

The adjusted EBITDA margin trajectory is the mechanism through which the operating model becomes self-reinforcing at scale.

Nebius reported adjusted EBITDA margin on its core AI cloud segment of 19 percent in Q3 2025. In Q4 2025, [that figure expanded to 24 percent](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001513845/000110465925109806/tm2530882d1_ex99-1.htm) — a 5 percentage point sequential expansion as fixed operating costs distributed across a faster-growing revenue base. The FY2026 guidance targets approximately 40 percent — 16 percentage points above the Q4 exit rate.

The Q4 net loss of $249.6 million illustrates why the GAAP income statement is a lagging indicator at this stage. A significant portion reflects depreciation on infrastructure deployed ahead of the revenue curve and non-cash stock-based compensation.

## The Power Problem — and What It Signals

Connected power is the most legible proxy for execution progress available to external observers. Software and contractual commitments are difficult to audit; megawatts of activated data centre power are not.

Nebius reported 170 megawatts of active connected power at year-end 2025 against more than 2 gigawatts contracted. The FY2026 guidance calls for 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt active by year-end — a 4.7-fold to 5.9-fold expansion in twelve months, a rate with few precedents outside hyperscaler construction programmes.

The 2-gigawatt contracted figure provides a ceiling: Nebius has secured utility agreements and site commitments to support the guidance target. The execution question is whether activation can be paced to match Nvidia GPU delivery schedules and customer deployment timelines. The August 2025 Nvidia equity investment is directly relevant: a supplier with a financial stake in customer growth carries a material incentive to prioritise allocation requests.

At 170 megawatts active against 2 gigawatts contracted, Nebius ended 2025 with roughly 8.5 percent of contracted capacity producing revenue. The gap between that figure and the 40-percent EBITDA margin target describes the entire financial story — a company that has secured commitments far in excess of its current operating footprint and is committing $3.7 billion of cash plus the most aggressive guidance in the sector to the proposition that the activation curve will prove as steep as projections require.

chapters.title: From restructuring print to first-billion ARR
chapters.body:
## The opening prints: out of the restructuring window

When Nebius disclosed its earliest post-restructuring quarterly results through 2025, the numbers were, by design, modest. The company that emerged from the 2024 separation was not a going concern with a seasoned customer base — it was a holding company with a GPU-cluster footprint in European data centres and a thesis about what AI infrastructure demand would look like at scale.

The early 2025 quarters told a familiar build-ahead story. Revenue scaled from a small base as the company signed its initial enterprise AI customers and began converting contracted commitments into recognised revenue under IFRS. What distinguished Nebius was not the pace of early revenue — it was the scale of the infrastructure commitment being built ahead of it.

## August 2025: the capital event that reset the narrative

The most consequential capital-markets event of Nebius's post-restructuring life was the August 2025 $700 million strategic equity placement. The placement's oversubscription was itself a signal, but Nvidia's participation carried the most structural weight.

Nvidia was simultaneously Nebius's dominant GPU supplier and, from August 2025 forward, a strategic equity investor. That alignment created circular reinforcement: an equity stake gives Nvidia a financial interest in Nebius's capacity ramp succeeding, which shapes GPU allocation priority during periods of constrained supply.

Accel's participation arrived with governance consequences: Matt Weigand received observer rights and was subsequently elected to the board alongside Arne Grimme at the August 2025 AGM.

## Q3 2025: the trajectory clarifies

By Q3 2025, annualised recurring revenue had approached approximately $700 million — a meaningful acceleration from the early-year base. [Source: Nebius 6-K, SEC EDGAR] The core AI cloud segment was growing faster than the consolidated entity, as the portfolio subsidiaries contributed at materially lower growth rates. The margin trajectory was improving: adjusted EBITDA margin for the core segment reached 19% in Q3.

Each quarterly disclosure was read not for its absolute revenue number but for the acceleration implied in the ARR trajectory and the physical capacity being brought online behind it.

## February 12, 2026: the earnings release as inflection event

The Q4 2025 results, released February 12, 2026, reframed the entire preceding year as prologue. [Source: Nebius Group, Business Wire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results)

Consolidated quarterly revenue came in at $227.7 million, representing 547% year-on-year growth. The core AI cloud segment posted 802% year-on-year growth. The exit ARR reached $1.25 billion, up from the approximate $700 million annualised run-rate of Q3.

The headline revenue figure was, on its own terms, a miss — analyst consensus had stood at roughly $247 million. In practice, the market's reaction was subordinated to what management disclosed alongside it: the margin expansion (Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin to 24%, up from Q3's 19%), the operating cash flow signature, and the forward guidance.

The Q4 operating cash flow of $834 million against $227.7 million of revenue — nearly four dollars of operating cash inflow for every dollar of recognised revenue — was the clearest expression of the customer prepayment dynamic. Enterprise AI customers booking large compute contracts prepay for capacity; the cash arrives before revenue is recognised under IFRS.

## The FY2026 guidance

The targets management set placed Nebius in a category of its own among publicly listed AI-cloud peers.

| Metric | FY2025 (Q4 / Exit) | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Quarterly revenue | $227.7M (+547% YoY) | — |
| Full-year revenue | — | $3.0–3.4B |
| Adj. EBITDA margin (core) | 24% (Q4 exit) | ~40% |
| Year-end ARR | $1.25B | $7–9B |
| Capex | ~$2B in Q4 alone | $16–20B |
| Connected power (active) | 170MW | 800MW–1GW |

The ARR target of $7 to $9 billion, with more than half already contracted at guidance disclosure, provided demand-side visibility unusual in AI-cloud forward guidance. The greater-than-50% contracted share translated the range from speculative pipeline estimate into an execution question: could Nebius deploy capacity fast enough to satisfy commitments already on paper?

## Seven quarters in: a compression without precedent

Taken across seven public quarters since the Nebius brand was established, the narrative is one of unusual compression. The company executed a corporate restructuring while simultaneously rebuilding a balance sheet, constructing an AI-cloud infrastructure footprint, recruiting a customer base capable of generating $1.25 billion in ARR, and closing strategically consequential equity financing.

Nebius did not accelerate an existing AI-cloud business — it built one inside a restructured holding company while that company was simultaneously resolving its post-Yandex governance architecture. The February 12, 2026 earnings release was the moment the sum of those parts became legible as a single coherent story: a corporate reorganisation that had, inside seven public quarters, become one of the most aggressive AI-infrastructure-capacity expansion narratives in the public-equity cycle.

chapters.title: Yandex legacy plus the Accel-and-Nvidia-aligned new arrivals
chapters.body:
## The Founder Returns

When Arkady Volozh walked back through the door in 2024, he carried something no hire could replicate: he had built the original company from a CompTek incubator project into one of Europe's most sophisticated technology organisations, led it through a 2011 NASDAQ listing that valued it at more than $8 billion, and shepherded the international asset base through the most turbulent period in Russian corporate history. His 2022 departure — made in the context of post-invasion political pressure, with Volozh publicly condemning the war in Ukraine — had been framed as severance from the Russian state machinery his company had become entangled with. His return reframed that departure as prelude rather than epilogue.

The corporate structure Volozh returned to lead was a product of controlled demolition and reconstruction. Nebius Group N.V. was effectively a blank-slate vehicle carrying one critical asset: a balance sheet that held $3.7 billion in cash by year-end 2025 and had generated $834 million in Q4 operating cash flow. That financial foundation, combined with Volozh's institutional credibility, allowed the company to recruit capital at scale: a $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement from Accel, Nvidia, and Orbis in August 2025.

## The Institutional Memory Layer

John Boynton had been in the room before Yandex was Yandex. In 1990, he co-founded CompTek International, the company that incubated Yandex itself. He has sat on the board continuously since 2000 and became chairman in 2016 — meaning he held the chair through the 2022 invasion, the prolonged restructuring negotiation, and the 2024 transformation that produced Nebius Group. That unbroken continuity represents institutional knowledge that no external appointment could substitute.

Outside his Nebius role, Boynton remains active in early-stage technology through Firehouse Capital and recently co-founded Litix, a vertical SaaS AI company targeting public-sector organisations — a contemporary signal that the chairman of a company pursuing an aggressive AI infrastructure thesis is himself building an AI application business.

Charles Ryan's connection runs through the original financing: in 1998, while co-running United Financial Group, he sponsored early-stage investment through ru-Net Holdings that included Yandex. He joined the board at the 2011 NASDAQ IPO. His career traced the arc of Western financial engagement with Russia: EBRD privatisation work, UFG founding, Deutsche Bank Russia CEO from 2005 to 2008. His contemporary role as General Partner at Almaz Capital Partners — a Silicon Valley venture firm positioned around US-Eastern Europe technology connections — makes him an active conduit for the engineering-talent and deal-flow networks Nebius is attempting to reconstitute.

## The Legal Architecture

Ophir Nave joined as Chief Operating Officer in May 2024 and was elected Executive Director at the August 2024 AGM. His credentials were calibrated for the task: Doctor of Juridical Science from Harvard Law School, Israeli Supreme Court clerkship, Wachtell Lipton Rosen & Katz, and lead partnership in the Corporate and M&A practice at Arnon Tadmor-Levy. The assembly of a Netherlands-incorporated public company retaining international technology assets from a Russian operating entity while maintaining a NASDAQ listing is a feat of cross-border legal engineering; Nave's credential set explains how it was executed.

## The Science and Education Thread

Elena Bunina joined the board as Non-Executive Director in August 2024, simultaneously in her operational role as Head of Science and Education. An Israel-based mathematician with close to seventy research publications, she previously served as Head of Academic and Educational Services across the Yandex Group and, until April 2022, as both General Director and Director of Human Resources at Yandex LLC. Her role connects directly to TripleTen and the company's longer-term positioning in AI talent development.

## The AI-Domain and Governance Additions

Kira Radinsky joined as an Independent Non-Executive Director in 2024. As CEO and Chairwoman of Diagnostic Robotics and founder of Mana Bio, her operational experience is in building and leading AI application businesses. The prior SalesPredict/eBay trajectory provides successful AI-startup exit pattern recognition. For a board evaluating AI infrastructure investment decisions that will be measured against AI application customer performance, having a director who has been on both sides of the infrastructure-application divide carries specific utility.

The August 2025 AGM brought two additions representing the governance consequences of the $700 million financing.

Arne Grimme, partner at De Brauw Blackstone Westbroek leading its Corporate M&A practice, provides Netherlands-domicile governance expertise. Nebius is an N.V. incorporated under Dutch law; Grimme's appointment anchors that expertise into the boardroom.

Matthew Weigand, an Accel partner since 2013 focusing on enterprise software, financial technology, and security, joined concurrent with Accel's participation in the strategic placement. He had held observer rights prior to formal election. The Accel/Nvidia dual participation signalled that sophisticated enterprise-technology investors had underwritten the AI-infrastructure thesis alongside the hardware supplier.

## The Board as Strategic Blueprint

| Director | Role | Primary Credential for Nebius |
|---|---|---|
| Arkady Volozh | CEO, Executive Director | Founder; institutional credibility |
| John Boynton | Independent Non-Executive Chairman | CompTek co-founder; board since 2000 |
| Charles E. Ryan | Independent Non-Executive Director | Russia-finance bridge; 2011 IPO continuity |
| Ophir Nave | COO, Executive Director | Harvard SJD + Wachtell M&A; legal architect |
| Elena Bunina | Head of Science & Education, Non-Executive Director | Mathematician; 70 publications; education pipeline |
| Kira Radinsky | Independent Non-Executive Director | Diagnostic Robotics CEO; AI-domain expertise |
| Arne Grimme | Independent Non-Executive Director | De Brauw partner; Dutch corporate M&A |
| Matthew Weigand | Independent Non-Executive Director | Accel partner; $700M placement co-investor |

The three Yandex-legacy figures — Boynton, Ryan, and Volozh — supply institutional memory and credibility required to maintain a NASDAQ listing through exceptional corporate transformation. The five newer arrivals each map onto specific strategic requirements: Nave built the legal form, Bunina manages the talent pipeline, Radinsky provides AI-domain pattern recognition, Grimme embeds Dutch governance expertise, and Weigand brings the venture governance and co-investor alignment signal.

The Accel and Nvidia placement, consummated in August 2025, crystallised the narrative. A company running $1.25 billion in ARR at year-end 2025 and targeting $7 to $9 billion by end-2026 requires more than a capable CEO and strong balance sheet. It requires a board whose composition can independently validate each component of that thesis to institutional investors. The structure Volozh assembled is that validation made organisational.

chapters.title: Hyperscaler-adjacent customers, Nvidia-aligned supply
chapters.body:
## Who Was Buying — and Why That Mattered

Nebius did not publish a customer list. That was not an oversight. It was characteristic of the segment it had chosen to serve.

The enterprise AI infrastructure market operates through multi-year framework agreements signed under non-disclosure — a contracting culture imported from the hyperscalers whose overflow Nebius was explicitly designed to absorb. The company described its customer base in structural terms rather than by name: AI laboratories and foundation-model developers consuming GPU compute for training runs; multi-cloud enterprise buyers requiring burst capacity outside a primary hyperscaler relationship; and production inference customers seeking guaranteed resource availability.

What Nebius's disclosure did confirm — in the [February 2026 Q4 earnings release](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results) — was that more than half of its $7–9 billion FY2026 ARR target was already contracted. That single data point defined revenue quality in a way customer names could not.

The distinction between contracted ARR and spot-market GPU cloud revenue is not cosmetic. Spot AI cloud markets carry structural churn risk tied to model-training cycles, lab funding cycles, and capacity overhang from incumbent hyperscalers. Multi-year commercial commitments from enterprise buyers provide revenue visibility more common to enterprise software than cloud infrastructure at equivalent growth rates. The $834 million in Q4 operating cash flow against $227.7 million in revenue reflects customer prepayments accruing well ahead of recognised revenue — a signature of hyperscaler-style commercial terms.

## The Nvidia Equation

No single relationship carries as much strategic weight as the one with Nvidia.

In August 2025, Nebius closed a $700 million [oversubscribed strategic equity placement](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-announces-oversubscribed-strategic-equity-financing-of-usd-700-million-to-accelerate-roll-out-of-full-stack-ai-infrastructure), with Nvidia participating alongside Accel and Orbis Investments. The placement was not passive financial investment. Nvidia's decision to take an equity stake in an AI cloud company — while simultaneously being the dominant GPU supplier — created alignment that constrains how to think about Nebius's supply position.

The company did not publicly disclose specific allocation terms or volumes. What is visible is the broader logic: a GPU supplier that holds equity in a customer has interests diverging from a purely transactional relationship. The implication — preferential allocation treatment within Nvidia's constrained GPU output pipeline — was broadly understood as a practical benefit of the structure.

Nvidia's roadmap — H100/H200 through Blackwell B100/B200 and into Rubin — is the backbone of every serious AI cloud capacity plan. The allocation question — who receives priority in a supply-constrained environment — is the defining competitive variable for independent operators. Nebius's placement inserted Nvidia as a financial co-owner at a moment when Nebius was planning the most aggressive capex program any AI-cloud company had publicly committed to.

## Power as the Binding Constraint

If GPU allocation is the most consequential uncertainty, power is the slowest-moving constraint.

Nebius exited 2025 with 170 megawatts of connected power against more than 2,000 megawatts under contract. That gap is a map of the construction pipeline. Power utility agreements, site acquisitions, grid interconnections, cooling infrastructure, and data centre build-out each carry their own lead times, regulatory dependencies, and execution risk. The FY2026 target of 800–1,000 megawatts represents a five- to six-fold physical expansion in a single year.

Nebius's European footprint — centred on Finland, where legacy Yandex infrastructure provides a starting base — is being supplemented by US site development. The practical execution sequence is constrained by physics rather than capital. Money can accelerate site acquisition and vendor commitments. It cannot compress utility interconnection timelines or lead times on large-format cooling deployments.

The hardware supply chain between GPU procurement and operational data centre capacity includes Supermicro, Dell, HPE, and contract manufacturers including Foxconn-FII. These are not differentiated relationships — they are the standard supply chain for any company purchasing Nvidia GPU clusters at scale. The differentiation resides upstream, in the Nvidia relationship, and downstream, in the contracted customer base.

## The Investor Constellation

The three co-investors in the August 2025 placement read as a deliberate construction.

Accel brought enterprise software credibility and an AI-infrastructure portfolio complementing Nebius's positioning. The placement brought Accel partner Matthew Weigand onto the board — an observer seat that converted to formal election at the August 2025 AGM.

Orbis Investments added a different dimension. Orbis's capital profile — patient, multi-year, drawn to structural re-ratings — suggests the placement attracted investors whose time horizon matches the construction cycle rather than quarterly earnings cadence.

Nvidia's role has been discussed above. The combination produced a $700 million placement that was simultaneously strategic validation, supplier-alignment signal, and capital-structure reinforcement.

## Positioned but Not Moated

The competitive framing requires intellectual honesty about the nature of Nebius's advantages.

| Operator | Status | Balance Sheet | Nvidia Alignment | Power (Active) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nebius (NBIS) | Public, NASDAQ | $3.7B cash | Strategic equity investor | 170MW → 800-1,000MW guided |
| CoreWeave (CRWV) | Public, NASDAQ | More leveraged | Deep procurement relationship | Larger active footprint |
| Lambda | Private | VC-backed | Nvidia-aligned | Undisclosed |
| Crusoe | Private | VC-backed | Nvidia-aligned | Differentiated power source |
| Azure AI / GCP / AWS | Internal divisions | Balance-sheet unlimited | Preferred customer status | Multi-gigawatt at scale |

Nebius is differentiated by cash position and formalised Nvidia equity alignment. These are real advantages. They are not irreplaceable moats. CoreWeave has a larger active deployment base. The hyperscalers have unlimited capital and existing customer relationships. Lambda and Crusoe compete for the same AI-lab customers.

The structural observation that matters: the case for Nebius's FY2026 targets rests on three things executing concurrently — GPU allocations arriving on schedule, power infrastructure commissioning at the required rate, and contracted customers drawing against committed obligations. Each is plausible on available evidence. None is guaranteed. The FY2026 guidance window is simultaneously the company's strongest commercial signal and most demanding operational test.

chapters.title: Where Nebius sits in the AI cloud landscape
chapters.body:
The AI infrastructure market that Nebius entered under its new identity in 2024 was already contested, capital-intensive, and structurally stratified. Three distinct competitive tiers had formed: hyperscalers commanding the top through integrated cloud platforms of oceanic scale; a mid-tier of pure-play AI GPU clouds accumulating Nvidia hardware and customer contracts; and a lower tier of regional or specialty operators seeking to monetise geographic or power advantages. Nebius sat squarely in the second tier — but the ambition encoded in its guidance placed it on a trajectory designed to compress that distance.

## The Three-Tier Landscape

The top tier belongs to Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Amazon Web Services. These are not competitors Nebius confronts directly for the same customer dollar, at least not in a symmetric sense. The hyperscalers' AI cloud capacity is embedded inside broader cloud relationships that include data storage, managed databases, identity, productivity software, and decades of enterprise integration. A Nebius customer buys AI GPU compute. A Microsoft Azure customer buys AI GPU compute alongside everything else. The competitive pressure from the hyperscaler tier is therefore a gravitational field rather than head-to-head battle: it sets the price floor, the service-level expectations, and the default procurement option for largest enterprises.

The regional and specialty tier — Foxconn-FII's cloud manufacturing partnerships, Equinix's AI Labs, national-champion clouds operated by Telefónica, Orange, and Deutsche Telekom — occupies different competitive space. Their advantages are geographic proximity to regulated jurisdictions (GDPR, DORA, NIS2), local language support, and pre-existing carrier relationships. Their disadvantage is GPU allocation: without Nvidia's direct strategic alignment, access to newest accelerator generations flows later, in smaller quantities, and at higher cost.

The operative contest for Nebius is the middle tier: the pure-play AI GPU clouds where capital deployment speed, Nvidia relationship depth, data centre power, and customer contract quality determine who survives the consolidation expected by 2027.

## The Pure-Play Peer Set

At the snapshot date, the principal competitors in the pure-play tier were CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV), Lambda (private), Crusoe (private), and Vultr (private). Each had assembled Nvidia GPU clusters, built or leased data centre capacity, and competed for the same AI-lab and enterprise-ML customers.

| Company | Status | Balance-sheet posture | Nvidia relationship | Active capacity (est.) | ARR visibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CoreWeave | Public (CRWV) | Highly leveraged; asset-backed debt | Strategic alignment; among largest customers | Larger than Nebius at snapshot | Large contracted backlog |
| **Nebius** | **Public (NBIS)** | **$3.7B cash; low leverage** | **Equity investor (Aug 2025)** | **170MW exit-2025** | **>50% of $7–9B FY26 ARR contracted** |
| Lambda | Private | VC-backed | Nvidia-aligned | Undisclosed | Undisclosed |
| Crusoe | Private | VC-backed; differentiated power | Nvidia-aligned | Undisclosed | Undisclosed |
| Vultr | Private | Bootstrapped | Standard procurement | Smaller scale | Undisclosed |

The comparison with CoreWeave crystallises the two dominant models. CoreWeave built scale earlier through asset-backed credit facilities, treating Nvidia hardware as collateral like aircraft lessors treat jet engines. By the snapshot date, CoreWeave's active deployed capacity exceeded Nebius's materially. But the debt load distinguishes the balance sheets sharply.

Nebius entered 2026 with $3.7 billion in cash and Q4 operating cash flow reflecting customer prepayments consistent with multi-year enterprise contracting. CoreWeave's balance sheet carries structurally different risk — GPU collateralisation is defensible while Nvidia hardware commands premium secondhand values, but that premium is not guaranteed across hardware generations as depreciation curves steepen.

Both share the most consequential fact in the pure-play tier: Nvidia's direct alignment. For Nebius, that alignment was formalised through equity ownership in August 2025. The practical consequence — while specific volumes were not disclosed — is a structural queue position that neither Lambda, Crusoe, nor Vultr has formalised at the same level.

## Structural Advantages

Nebius's competitive position rests on four pillars, each reinforcing the others.

**Balance-sheet depth.** A $3.7 billion cash position provides a multi-year runway that peers relying on debt financing or continued equity raises do not possess. Against $16–20 billion capex guidance, the cash covers less than a quarter — additional financing is an explicit requirement — but the starting position is among the cleanest in the peer set.

**Nvidia alignment.** When Nvidia invests in an AI cloud operator, it signals which operators the company expects to be significant buyers across a multi-year horizon. The circular logic — Nebius buys Nvidia hardware; Nvidia invests; Nebius can credibly signal GPU allocation priority to enterprise customers — creates compounding advantage a later-arriving competitor cannot replicate by simply writing a cheque.

**Geographic positioning.** The Netherlands domicile and European data centre footprint insulate the company from US export-control regime governing AI hardware shipments to China. For customers seeking non-US jurisdictional diversity, Nebius's European domicile is a genuine differentiator.

**Contracted revenue visibility.** The disclosure that more than half of the $7–9 billion FY2026 ARR target was already under contract meant Nebius's revenue execution risk was primarily a capacity-deployment risk — the question of whether the company can build fast enough to honour signed contracts — rather than demand-generation risk.

## Structural Disadvantages

The counterweights are equally concrete.

Nebius's AI-infrastructure brand is younger than competitors'. CoreWeave has operated as a GPU cloud since 2017, building customer relationships across multiple hardware generations before Nebius had formalised its restructured identity. Lambda's origins in high-performance computing gave it technical reputation predating the AI supercycle. Nebius is, in operating terms, a 2024-vintage AI cloud company housed inside a decades-old corporate structure.

The capex mathematics are severe. Against $3.7 billion starting cash and $16–20 billion capex guidance, the financing requirement is roughly $12–16 billion. Nebius will need to access debt markets, issue additional equity, or both — at scale, in a capital environment watching CoreWeave's leverage structure and reassessing risk premium for hardware-collateralised AI cloud debt.

The three portfolio subsidiaries — Toloka AI, TripleTen, and Avride — are a source of managerial complexity pure-play competitors do not carry. Management cycles spent on an autonomous-driving venture and online coding bootcamp are cycles not spent on data centre site selection, power utility negotiations, and GPU cluster deployment.

The corporate restructuring overhang persists as a buyer-base constraint. Some allocators, constrained by Russia-related sanctions policy or ESG mandates, remain cautious regardless of operating performance. The overhang did not impede the August 2025 $700 million placement, but it continues to narrow the natural buyer base.

## The Execution Crucible

If Nebius executes against FY2026 targets, the outcome is a step-change in tier positioning. A company generating $7–9 billion of annualised recurring revenue from AI cloud infrastructure — with more than half contracted in advance — would represent scale comparable to the lower bound of what hyperscalers deploy internally, and the largest capitalised pure-play AI GPU cloud in public markets.

If Nebius misses materially, the remaining assets are still substantial: cash, Nvidia equity alignment, European data centre footprint, and contracted customer base. What would not survive intact is the operational thesis — that Volozh's team can deploy capacity at a rate no AI cloud company has previously attempted in a single fiscal year, while managing three subsidiaries and a freshly restructured corporate identity.

The competitive position is best understood not as a static ranking but as an option on a tier-leapfrog. The structural advantages are real, defensible, and in several cases unique. The execution bar attached to exercising that option is correspondingly severe.

chapters.title: From restructuring close to $700M financing
chapters.body:
## The Restructuring Close: A Netherlands Holdco Reborn

The paperwork that closed in 2024 was, in its legal form, a divestiture. In its strategic consequence, it was closer to a founding act. When Yandex N.V. completed the sale of its Russian operating business to a consortium of domestic investors, what remained was a deliberately stripped-down collection of international holdings. The entity was rebranded Nebius Group N.V. and its NASDAQ ticker changed to NBIS.

The restructuring also brought back the one executive whose return sent the most unambiguous signal. Arkady Volozh's return to the operational helm was the company's most direct statement that the reconstituted entity was not a liquidating holdco but a going concern executing a specific technology bet.

## Board Reconstruction: New Faces for a New Mandate

The governance rebuild reflected that bet. John Boynton — board member since 2000 and chairman since 2016 — provided institutional continuity. Around that anchor, the company assembled a board configured for AI-infrastructure oversight.

Ophir Nave joined as Chief Operating Officer in May 2024, formalised with an Executive Director board seat in August 2024. Elena Bunina joined as a Non-Executive Director at the same August 2024 tranche, taking responsibility for Nebius Science and Education. Kira Radinsky rounded out the 2024 additions as an Independent Non-Executive Director, bringing AI-domain credibility.

## The August 2025 Placement

By mid-2025, the infrastructure ramp was consuming capital at a rate requiring additional financing. The August 2025 $700 million strategic equity placement, [described by the company as oversubscribed](https://nebius.com/newsroom/nebius-announces-oversubscribed-strategic-equity-financing-of-usd-700-million-to-accelerate-roll-out-of-full-stack-ai-infrastructure), brought three named investors: Accel, Nvidia, and certain accounts managed by Orbis Investments.

At the August 2025 AGM, shareholders elected Arne Grimme and Matthew Weigand to the board. Grimme cemented Netherlands-domicile governance architecture; Weigand formalised Accel's alignment.

## The February 2026 Print: First Public Proof Point

On February 12, 2026, [Nebius reported Q4 and full-year 2025 results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results). The numbers removed ambiguity about ambitions. The Q4 revenue came in below consensus expectations of ~$247 million — the miss mattered less than the direction of travel.

| Metric | Q4 2025 |
|---|---|
| Revenue | $227.7M |
| Core AI Cloud Segment | +802% YoY |
| Adj. EBITDA Margin (core) | 24% |
| Operating Cash Flow | $834M |
| Capex | ~$2.0B |
| Exit ARR | $1.25B |
| Year-End Cash | $3.7B |
| Active Power | 170MW |
| Contracted Power | >2,000MW |

## Forward Catalysts

At the snapshot date of May 23, 2026, several catalysts remained in the pipeline. The Q1 2026 6-K had not yet entered the public record. That filing would provide the first quarterly data point on whether the revenue ramp was tracking guidance: a trajectory consistent with $3.0–3.4 billion full-year revenue required approximately $700–800 million in Q1.

Beyond quarterly cadence, the catalysts that matter most are operational: data centre commissioning announcements (public confirmation that specific sites moved from contracted to active power); customer design-win disclosures to the extent contracting structure permits; additional strategic financing to address the gap between cash and capex guidance; and any Nvidia roadmap alignment announcement confirming GPU allocation across Blackwell or Rubin generations.

## Specialist Commentary

The public discourse around Nebius's equity story had coalesced around consistent structural framing: the core bull argument held that Nebius occupied a differentiated position — not a pure-play GPU-rental business but a full-stack infrastructure operator whose balance sheet, strategic supply alignment, and contracted ARR visibility constituted advantages more leveraged competitors could not replicate. The corporate-restructuring narrative was typically treated as context rather than thesis: the Yandex origin mattered for understanding management depth and European footprint, but FY2026 guidance and the Nvidia circular alignment drove forward analysis.

chapters.title: From Yandex Cloud to full-stack AI infrastructure
chapters.body:
## The inherited stack

When Nebius emerged from the 2024 restructuring, it retained something more durable than balance-sheet cash: two decades of production-grade cloud engineering built to serve one of the world's most demanding domestic internet markets. Yandex Cloud had been engineered to hyperscaler tolerances without hyperscaler margins. That engineering culture, and the international teams who built the most technically sophisticated parts, stayed with the Amsterdam-domiciled holdco.

The software and orchestration layers Nebius inherited were not greenfield AI-cloud constructs but battle-hardened commodity. Yandex had operated its own bare-metal orchestration, custom networking fabrics, and storage systems at scale for a decade. The 2024 divestiture stripped the Russia-specific operating layer and left the international engineering team intact.

## Engineering geography

Nebius's engineering footprint is deliberately distributed across jurisdictions providing both talent access and geopolitical optionality. The corporate domicile sits in the Netherlands, functioning as a holding and governance layer. Finland represents the legacy physical anchor — the data centre infrastructure providing the initial capacity base. Israel is a material engineering node, with several core engineering functions staffed from the Israeli technology ecosystem. US expansion was underway by end-2025, representing the most commercially significant geographic extension.

## Toloka AI: the data-layer asset

Toloka AI, the crowd-sourced human-data labelling platform, is the group's most underappreciated IP asset in public commentary. Global-scale data labelling — producing high-quality annotated training data — is technically and operationally non-trivial. Toloka had been built by Yandex as an internal data-quality engine before productisation. Its global worker network and quality-assurance tooling represent a meaningful complement to the core AI cloud: customers training large models on Nebius compute can, in principle, close the data-to-training loop within the same vendor relationship.

## Avride: the long-cycle bet

Avride, the autonomous driving technology subsidiary, is the group's longest-duration R&D commitment. The technology development cycles are measured in years, and regulatory pathways add further lag. Nebius treats Avride's expenditure as operating expense rather than capitalised development cost — a conservative accounting treatment flowing directly through the group's consolidated net loss line.

The strategic logic of retention is that autonomous driving will eventually require exactly the kind of compute infrastructure Nebius is building — maintaining the capability in-house preserves optionality.

## The Nvidia layer and the orchestration moat

The most consequential IP relationship is not a patent portfolio or proprietary software stack — it is the Nvidia strategic alignment. In a market where GPU allocation is the primary constraint on AI-cloud capacity, a strategic investor relationship with the dominant hardware supplier provides preferential queue access that no software patent can replicate.

Nebius's actual IP leverage — like CoreWeave, Lambda, or Crusoe — lies in the orchestration, infrastructure management, and operational layers above GPU silicon. Customers run their own workloads on Nvidia hardware that Nebius procures, deploys, and operates. The defensible value is in the ability to deploy that hardware faster, more reliably, and with better utilisation economics than alternatives. Yandex Cloud's engineering heritage — particularly in networking, storage, and bare-metal orchestration — is the substrate.

On patents: Yandex-legacy intellectual property did flow into Nebius post-restructuring. However, specific count and category breakdown had not been surfaced in public filings at the snapshot date.

## The open moat question

The central strategic question is whether operational excellence at AI cloud scale — plus a privileged Nvidia GPU allocation pipeline — converts into a durable competitive position, or whether it represents a first-mover window that hyperscaler internal capacity and well-capitalised peers will eventually close.

The contracted ARR visibility provides near-term revenue predictability. What it does not resolve is the longer-duration question: whether the orchestration and operational IP constitutes a moat that scales as underlying hardware commoditises. That question remained open at the snapshot date.

chapters.title: Capex bar, customer concentration, and the restructuring overhang
chapters.body:
## The arithmetic of the build

The most consequential number in Nebius's FY2026 guidance is not the revenue figure or the ARR target. It is the gap between two other figures: the $16–20 billion capital expenditure programme and the $3.7 billion of cash at year-end 2025. That gap — $12 to $16 billion — has to be filled by operating cash generation, debt, and further equity issuance.

The Q4 2025 operating cash flow of $834 million reflects prepayment structure of enterprise AI cloud contracts more than underlying earnings capacity. Even annualising generously, that covers perhaps $3–3.5 billion of annual operating cash flow. The remainder requires external financing at scale and pace no other AI infrastructure company has attempted.

The company has not been silent on this. The August 2025 $700 million placement was structured to finance the infrastructure ramp. The prepayment profile provides partial self-financing. But the capex guidance implies raising additional capital against a macro backdrop it cannot control.

**Leading indicator:** The pace and terms of any debt facility announced in 2026, and whether management revises capex guidance toward the $16 billion floor. A narrowing of the range or public acknowledgment of phasing would signal the financing constraint is binding.

## Concentrated demand, undisclosed names

Nebius disclosed that more than half of its $7–9 billion FY2026 ARR target is already contracted. That disclosure carries two distinct readings. The optimistic reading is de-risked forward revenue, converting pipeline into legally committed obligations. The cautious reading: because customer names are not disclosed, the contracted book could be highly concentrated, and a single large cancellation would materially reduce the ARR figure.

The prepayment structure shapes the concentration risk. Enterprise AI cloud contracts typically involve staged or upfront payments tied to capacity reservation. That structure gives cash visibility but creates asymmetric exposure: if a large customer renegotiates, consequences extend beyond lost revenue into potential repayment obligations against prepaid amounts. The company has not publicly quantified exposure to any single customer.

Management's stated mitigation is breadth and diversity of the contracted book — implying multiple counterparties rather than a single anchor tenant. The comparator is CoreWeave, which disclosed significant revenue concentration in Microsoft Azure during its IPO process.

**Leading indicator:** Any disclosure of customer-count data in subsequent 6-K filings would immediately reprice concentration risk.

## The Nvidia alignment that is not a guarantee

Nvidia's August 2025 equity participation was the most consequential validation event in Nebius's post-restructuring history. It signalled that the world's dominant GPU supplier was prepared to commit its own capital to a customer relationship.

The nuance matters. Strategic equity alignment is not contractual allocation guarantee. Nvidia sells GPUs to many customers simultaneously. If Nvidia faces a demand shock — whether from accelerated hyperscaler capex or compression in AI infrastructure demand — its allocation decisions will be driven by commercial and strategic calculus that Nebius's equity relationship influences but does not determine.

Each GPU architecture transition — H100/H200 to Blackwell to Rubin — creates a re-negotiation point in the allocation relationship, and each new generation involves production ramp dynamics outside Nebius's control.

**Leading indicator:** Any meaningful delay in the connected power ramp from 170MW to 800–1000MW would, absent stated financing problems, point toward hardware-supply bottleneck.

## Power as the rate-limiting constraint

The power infrastructure gap is the most straightforward risk to quantify and hardest to accelerate. Reaching 800–1,000 megawatts from 170 megawatts in twelve months requires roughly fivefold expansion — gated not by capital or GPU allocation, but by utility deployment timelines.

Power utility agreements are long-dated, slow-moving contracts with engineering lead times measured in years. Nebius's European footprint benefits from Finland's mature grid and cheap hydroelectric power. The US expansion operates in a power environment under sustained pressure from AI infrastructure build, with interconnection queues in major markets running multiple years.

The 2,000+ megawatts of contracted capacity represents future optionality across sites at different development stages.

**Leading indicator:** Quarterly active-versus-contracted power disclosures. Stagnation in the active power figure would signal timeline compression.

## The restructuring ghost

Nebius is, by legal construction, a clean successor entity. The 2024 restructuring separated Russian operations from the Netherlands holdco retaining international assets. Volozh returned as CEO in 2024, and the August 2025 Accel placement put a top-tier Silicon Valley firm's partner on the board.

None of that fully neutralises institutional screening. A meaningful subset of large investors — pension funds, sovereign wealth, ESG-screened mandates — maintain Russia-related governance filters flagging any entity with Yandex lineage, regardless of legal separation. The consequence is not existential but does constrain the demand side of future equity issuance.

**Leading indicator:** 13-F institutional ownership mix broadening beyond the initial August 2025 cohort.

## Demand cycle, management bandwidth, and regulatory perimeter

Three further risks sit in the background.

**Macro:** The AI infrastructure capex cycle underlying Nebius's demand story is itself a function of sustained hyperscaler AI spending. If hyperscaler capex compressed materially, the market for third-party AI GPU cloud would contract; the contracted ARR provides insulation, not permanent immunity.

**Internal:** Nebius consolidates three portfolio businesses alongside the core AI cloud. Avride is a long-cycle autonomous-driving R&D commitment with burn profile in uncomfortable contrast to quarterly-cadence AI cloud growth. The management bandwidth argument is that the core operation requires extraordinary execution focus at precisely the moment the portfolio adds complexity.

**Jurisdictional:** Nebius is Netherlands-domiciled, operates across multiple geographies, and faces emerging EU AI Act compliance requirements. None is acute at the snapshot date, but compliance overhead scales with the capex programme.

| Risk category | Specific exposure | Leading indicator |
|---|---|---|
| Capex financing | $12–16B gap beyond starting cash | Debt facility terms; guidance revision |
| Customer concentration | >50% contracted ARR, no named customers | Customer-count disclosure in 6-K |
| Nvidia GPU allocation | Strategic equity ≠ contractual priority | Active-power ramp pace |
| Power infrastructure | 170MW to 800–1,000MW target | Quarterly active-power disclosure |
| Restructuring overhang | Institutional governance filters | 13-F ownership broadening |
| AI capex cycle | Demand depends on hyperscaler spending | Hyperscaler AI capex guidance |
| Management bandwidth | Avride / TripleTen / Toloka alongside core | Avride strategic update or divestiture |
| Regulatory / tax | Netherlands domicile, EU AI Act | Transfer-pricing or compliance disclosures |

The risk register is not a case against the thesis. It is the precise specification of what has to go right simultaneously. The contracted revenue base and cash are genuine structural advantages. Whether they are sufficient is the question the next four quarters will answer.

chapters.title: The FY2026 execution test
chapters.body:
## The numbers on the table

When Nebius reported its [Q4 and FY2025 results](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260212534404/en/Nebius-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results), it set out an FY2026 operating plan with no precedent in the public-equity AI-infrastructure peer set: revenue guidance of $3.0–3.4 billion (~7x FY2025), capex guidance of $16–20 billion, ARR target of $7–9 billion with more than half contracted, and connected power scaling from 170 megawatts to 800–1,000 megawatts.

The guidance set the terms of a single, compressible question: whether Volozh's team can translate a balance sheet reconstituted from restructuring into the most aggressive AI-infrastructure capacity ramp any publicly listed company has committed to.

## The capex arithmetic

The internal logic of the $16–20 billion envelope is demanding. At flat distribution across four quarters, the midpoint implies $4–5 billion per quarter. Nebius spent approximately $2 billion on capex in Q4 2025 alone. The implication: Q2–Q4 2026 quarterly pace needs to double the Q4 2025 rate to hit the low end.

That acceleration is not incidental to the plan; it is the plan. AI-infrastructure build cycles do not permit gradual ramps. A site that slips its energisation date by one quarter does not catch up — the revenue it was intended to support does not compress into a smaller window.

The capex-to-revenue ratio at the revenue midpoint of $3.2 billion and capex midpoint of $18 billion is roughly 5.6x for the full year — infrastructure-ahead-of-demand spending at a scale previously associated only with hyperscalers themselves.

## Financing the build

The starting position is materially stronger than a year earlier. Year-end cash of $3.7 billion plus Q4 operating cash flow of $834 million (more than three times recognised revenue) reflects customer prepayment structure: buyers commit and pay ahead of capacity delivery.

If Q4's operating cash flow was sustained, annualised generation could approach or exceed $3 billion. Against $16–20 billion capex, however, cash plus operating cash flow covers at most the first two quarters at the required pace.

The arithmetic points to at least one additional capital-raise transaction during 2026. The August 2025 placement established that Nebius can access institutional capital at scale. The board composition — Grimme (Dutch corporate M&A specialist) and Weigand (Accel partner) — signals complex capital transactions are in prospect.

## The power constraint

Of the operational variables, the power ramp has the least managerial discretion. Moving from 170 megawatts to 800–1,000 megawatts is a 5–6x physical expansion. At roughly 200 megawatts per large-scale site, the midpoint implies four to five new sites reaching operational status through the year.

The company disclosed more than 2,000 megawatts of contracted power at end-2025 — the utility agreements and real-estate positions exist on paper. But the translation from contracted to connected is governed by grid interconnection queues, permitting processes, and construction schedules that respond to local conditions, not to guidance urgency.

## Operating leverage and the GAAP gap

The 40 percent adjusted EBITDA margin target at revenue midpoint implies approximately $1.3 billion in adjusted EBITDA for FY2026. That is a genuine operating leverage story: Q4 2025 adjusted EBITDA margin reached 24% (up from 19% in Q3), demonstrating revenue scale already converting to margin expansion.

GAAP profitability is a separate matter. A $16–20 billion capex programme will generate a depreciation wave dominating the GAAP income statement for years. GAAP profitability is not a feature of any plausible FY2026 scenario; adjusted EBITDA is the correct frame for evaluating cash-generative capacity.

| Metric | FY2025 (Q4 annualised) | FY2026 Guidance |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue | ~$910M run-rate | $3.0–3.4B |
| Adj. EBITDA margin (core) | ~24% | ~40% |
| Capex | ~$8B run-rate | $16–20B |
| Exit ARR | $1.25B | $7–9B (>50% contracted) |
| Connected power | 170MW | 800–1,000MW |

## Corporate optionality

Beyond the operational plan, Nebius carries strategic options whose exercise terms are undefined. The three portfolio subsidiaries — Toloka AI, TripleTen, and Avride — sit inside the consolidated group but operate as structurally separable businesses. None had disclosed a spin-out or IPO timeline at the snapshot date.

The board's composition can move on corporate transactions if conditions align. None of this constitutes a public signal of imminent action. The observation is structural: Nebius's board was not assembled for a steady-state operating company. It was assembled for a company in active strategic motion.

## The question Volozh hasn't answered yet

Every element of the FY2026 plan is internally coherent. The contracted ARR share reduces demand-side risk to levels no speculative-pipeline story could match. The Nvidia strategic-equity alignment provides the clearest available signal of GPU allocation priority. The cash base and operating cash flow generation provide financing depth. The board has transactional credentials to extend the runway.

What the plan cannot resolve in advance is sequencing risk between capital deployment and capacity delivery. Nebius is spending $16–20 billion to energise five or more data centre sites, ramp power by a factor of five, absorb GPU deliveries across multiple architectures, and convert contracted ARR into recognised revenue — all simultaneously.

The question is not whether individual components are achievable in isolation. It is whether Volozh's team can execute all of them in parallel, on the timeline guidance requires, while maintaining customer confidence.

That is the test FY2026 has set. The outcome will determine whether Nebius's three-part equity story — restructuring outcome, balance-sheet rebuild, AI-infrastructure ramp — resolves into a single coherent operating business, or whether one of the legs buckles under the weight of the most aggressive public-market AI-infrastructure commitment of the cycle.
